concept.technique_name: angle sum property with Pythagoras converse

examples.problem_statement: In \triangle ABC, \frac{\angle A}{\angle B} = 1 - \frac{\angle C}{\angle B}. Which of the following statements is true? (a) \triangle ABC is always an acute angled triangle (b) an angle exceeds 90^\circ (c) AB^2 + BC^2 = AC^2 (d) None of these

solution.operation: \frac{\angle A}{\angle B} \cdot \angle B = \left(1 - \frac{\angle C}{\angle B}\right) \cdot \angle B
solution.description: Clear the denominators by multiplying the given relation through by \angle B, turning the fractional condition into a plain relation among the three angles.

solution.result: \angle B equals the sum of the other two angles
solution.description: Move \angle C to the left side, so the condition now says that angle B alone accounts for as much as angles A and C together.

solution.result: the three angles of the triangle total 180^\circ
solution.description: Bring in the angle sum property of a triangle, the second fact needed alongside the relation just derived.
Substitute \angle A + \angle C = \angle B into the angle sum, replacing that pair by a single \angle B.
Halve both sides to isolate \angle B, which shows the triangle is right angled at B.
Apply Pythagoras at the right angle B: the two sides enclosing B are AB and BC, so their squares add to the square of the hypotenuse AC.

key_reminders: The angles of a triangle sum to 180^\circ.
If one angle equals the sum of the other two, that angle is 90^\circ.
In a right triangle the hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle, so the legs are the two sides meeting at it.
common_mistakes: Applying Pythagoras as AB^2 + AC^2 = BC^2, i.e. treating a leg as the hypotenuse instead of AC, which lies opposite the right angle at B.
Choosing (a) after seeing only that the relation is satisfiable, without deriving that \angle B is exactly 90^\circ, which rules out an acute triangle.

examples.problem_statement: The actress was desperate to (i) ___________ the part in the new Michel Gondry film. It was (ii) ___________ role, with lots of onscreen time and a number of long scenes that would allow the actress, usually cast as a vapid ingenue or bombshell, to truly show her dramatic range. Blank (i): land / ascertain / ensure. Blank (ii): a plum (among the choices offered).

solution.result: the target meaning for the first blank is fixed before looking at choices
solution.description: Read the first sentence and decide what the blank must mean: the actress is desperate to obtain the part, so the word has to be a synonym of get.
Substitute ascertain into the sentence and check the sense; it does not mean get, so it makes no sense here.

solution.operation: Test "ensure the part" against "ensure that she gets the part"
solution.result: ensure is rejected, leaving land for blank (i)
solution.description: Substitute ensure and notice it is used incorrectly: one can ensure that she gets the part, but not ensure the part itself, which eliminates the last rival.

solution.operation: Blank (ii) = a synonym of "good", matched to "a plum"
solution.result: a plum is chosen for blank (ii)
solution.description: Use the description that follows, lots of onscreen time and long showcase scenes, to set the second blank's target meaning as good, which is exactly what plum means.

key_reminders: Predict the meaning each blank needs from the sentence's own clues before evaluating the answer choices.
A choice must fit the exact grammatical object given, not a paraphrase you supply: ensure a clause is not ensure a noun.
The detail after the second blank (onscreen time, long scenes) is the clue that defines the required word.
common_mistakes: Picking ensure because the actress plausibly wants to ensure she gets the part, ignoring that the blank takes the part directly as its object.
Treating ascertain as a fancy synonym of obtain rather than of find out.

concept.technique_name: speed as distance over time with m/s to km/hr conversion

examples.problem_statement: How many km per hour does a man walk who passes through a street 600 m long in 5 minutes?

solution.description: Divide the distance in metres by the time expressed in seconds, converting the 5 minutes to 5 \times 60 seconds so that both quantities use base units.
Multiply the speed in m/s by 18/5, the standard factor that converts metres per second into kilometres per hour.
Write the improper fraction as a mixed number to state the walking speed in km/hr.

key_reminders: Speed = distance / time, with distance and time in matching units.
To convert m/s into km/hr multiply by 18/5.
common_mistakes: Dividing 600 by 5 and treating the result as m/s, forgetting to convert the 5 minutes into 300 seconds.
Multiplying by 5/18 instead of 18/5, which reverses the direction of the conversion.

solution.description: Multiply the fraction by 100 to express it as a percentage, cancelling the 8 against the 100 to leave 75/2.
Convert the improper fraction into a mixed number and attach the percent sign.

key_reminders: A fraction becomes a percentage when multiplied by 100.
Cancel before multiplying: 100 divided by 8 gives 25/2, which keeps the arithmetic small.
common_mistakes: Reporting 37 % and dropping the leftover half, since 75/2 is not a whole number.
